dedupe_keys.name: kenya 2024 floods loss of geographical access to public and private healthcare

description: This case study measures how the floods of April and May 2024 in Kenya cut people off from health facilities, compounded by a doctors' strike in the public sector. The authors published it as an open-access journal article. They assembled health facility locations for public, private not-for-profit and private for-profit providers, the road network, land use and land cover, topography, gridded population and flood extents mapped from Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar, and modelled travel time to the nearest facility for a pre-flood baseline and three post-flood scenarios. Coverage is all 47 counties of Kenya. The article is free under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Caveats: flood extents come from satellite snapshots, travel speeds are modelled, not observed, and facility functionality during the floods was inferred, not surveyed. The study found that before the floods 94.0 percent of the population, about 52.5 million people, lived within 30 minutes of care, and that flooding caused unequal losses of access across counties and sectors, with the longest post-flood travel times for private not-for-profit facilities; it concludes that Kenya's health system is highly vulnerable to floods. Simulation uses: an example of hazard exposure and resilience analysis of healthcare access, reusable as a template for flood scenarios elsewhere. Related records: the Kenya master health facility list (data-kenya-master-health-facility-list-2017), WorldPop gridded population (data-worldpop-global-gridded-population) and AccessMod (model-accessmod) cover comparable inputs and methods.
